blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Pathology foundation models supply strong representations for whole-slide image classification, yet the confidence attached to their predictions remains hard to trust. Prevailing uncertainty estimators act within a single feature space and thereby overlook the uncertainty that the choice of foundation-model representation itself induces. This work introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses several pathology foundation models for the specific purpose of uncertainty estimation. Departing from accuracy-driven fusion, CALIFUSE reads representational heterogeneity across encoders as an explicit confidence cue. Slide-level decision consensus is coupled with chunk-level evidence agreement quantified through Jensen-Shannon divergence, so that both prediction stability and fine-grained evidence consistency inform the estimate. Foundation-model encoders stay frozen. A task-specific nnMIL classifier is still trained for each FM; CALIFUSE then estimates confidence at inference without training an extra fusion module. Evaluated on seven WSI classification tasks under several foundation-model combinations, the framework sharpens calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction relative to both the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging, all while preserving competitive balanced accuracy.
blocks.zh: 病理基础模型为全塌方图像分类提供了强烈的表示,然而其预测所附带的信心仍然难以相信. 常见的不确定性估计器在一个单一的特征空间内行事,从而忽略了选择基础模型代表本身引起的不确定性。 这项工作引入了CALIFUSE,这是一个面向校准的框架,为不确定性估计的特定目的,将几种病理基础模型融合在一起。 脱离精度驱动的聚变,CALIFUSE将跨编码器的表征异质性视为一个明确的置信提示. 幻灯片级决策共识与通过Jensen-Shannon差异量化的块级证据协议相结合,从而使预测稳定性和精细证据一致性成为估计数的依据。 基金会模型编码器被冻结了 仍然为每个调频台培训一个任务特定的nnMIL分类器;然后,CALIFUSE在没有培训一个额外的聚变模块的情况下估算推断置信度. 对几个基础模型组合下的7个WSI分类任务进行了评价,框架比最强的单编码器基线和天真综艺平均率更精准,同时保持了竞争性平衡的准确性。

blocks.en:
Whole-slide image (WSI) analysis has moved away from training
slide classifiers from scratch. Contemporary pipelines encode gigapixel
tissue slides into transferable representations through pathology foundation
models (FMs), then couple these features with multiple-instance learning
(MIL) to produce slide-level predictions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Such designs
have advanced tumor subtyping, grading, and biomarker prediction. Clinical
deployment, however, is not served by accuracy in isolation. A useful model
must also recognize when its own answer is likely wrong, since the reported
confidence has to be trustworthy enough to underpin calibrated probability
estimation, error detection, and selective referral of difficult cases to
pathologists [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Within
computational pathology, uncertainty consequently ceases to be an auxiliary
statistic and becomes an integral part of the prediction.

blocks.en:
Most uncertainty estimation methods for WSI classification
remain confined to a single view. A fixed feature space is assumed, and
uncertainty is read off by perturbing the downstream predictor, resampling
patches, applying MC dropout, or invoking conformal and probabilistic MIL
variants [ 13 , 10 , 14 , 15 , 11 , 16 , 12 , 17 ] . Valuable
as these strategies are, they mainly quantify instability inside one
representation. Should the selected FM encode a biased, incomplete, or overly
smooth picture of the slide, the downstream predictor can remain internally
consistent yet overconfident. Put differently, single-FM uncertainty captures
ambiguity residing within a representation while overlooking the uncertainty
that the representation choice itself introduces.

blocks.en:
This gap is consequential because modern pathology FMs are
demonstrably heterogeneous, diverging in pretraining corpora, supervision
signals, magnification regimes, architecture, and morphological
priors [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 18 , 19 ] . One and
the same WSI may therefore appear straightforward in one feature space and
ambiguous in another. Prior multi-FM efforts have largely exploited such
heterogeneity in the service of accuracy, most often by fusing or averaging
predictions across models [ 20 , 21 ] . Averaging of this
kind, however, folds disagreement into a single posterior and can conceal
precisely the cases in which the system ought to hesitate. When strong FMs
part ways, their divergence is rarely mere noise to be damped out; more often
it constitutes a clinically meaningful indication that the case is borderline,
atypical, or underrepresented.

blocks.en:
A different question thus arises: can disagreement among
pathology foundation models be transformed into a calibrated uncertainty
signal? The answer pursued here is affirmative. This paper introduces CaliFuse , a calibration-oriented multi-foundation-model fusion framework
that treats such disagreement as informative in its own right and erects a
calibrated confidence estimate directly upon it. Two complementary signals are
combined. At the decision level, consensus among FM-specific
nnMIL [ 2 ] predictors is measured and
consensus-conditioned pooling is applied. At the evidence level,
Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence is computed over the chunk-level predictive
distributions emitted by every FM. The former signal records whether distinct
models reach the same slide-level decision; the latter records whether they
rest on compatible class evidence across the slide even when their top-1
labels coincide.

The results also delineate a nuanced boundary for the method.
Its advantages are most pronounced for error ranking and selective prediction,
whereas absolute calibration retains some dataset dependence; naive averaging,
for instance, edges ahead on Kidney ECE in the principal N = 5 N=5 setting. Rather
than a contradiction, this stands as an instructive takeaway: representational
disagreement is a potent uncertainty signal, even if deployments demanding
literal probabilities may still profit from an added post-hoc calibration
step [ 8 ] . Far from undermining the
argument, the observation reinforces the case for modeling heterogeneity
explicitly.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. Representational heterogeneity across pathology
foundation models is identified as an explicit and hitherto underused source
of uncertainty for WSI classification, moving multi-FM systems from
accuracy-oriented fusion toward calibration-oriented uncertainty estimation. 2. CaliFuse operationalizes this distinction through two
training-free confidence measures: consensus-conditioned pooling at the
decision level and Jensen–Shannon divergence over chunk-level predictive
distributions at the evidence level. 3. Extensive experiments over seven WSI tasks and several
fusion settings demonstrate that retaining cross-FM disagreement delivers
consistently stronger calibration and error ranking than both oracle
single-FM selection and naive probability averaging, without sacrificing
competitive slide-level classification.

blocks.en: II Related Work
blocks.zh: 二. 相关工作

blocks.en: II-A Pathology Foundation Models
blocks.zh: II-A 病理学基金会模型

blocks.en:
Self-supervised pretraining on large histology corpora has
established frozen patch encoders as a standard front end for WSI analysis.
UNI, trained by self-distillation on more than one hundred million patches
drawn from over one hundred thousand slides, transfers across a broad spectrum
of diagnostic tasks [ 6 ] . Virchow and its
mixed-magnification successor Virchow2 scale vision transformers to millions of
slides with an explicit focus on scale-heterogeneous
morphology [ 7 , 18 ] . Whole-slide
context is brought in by GigaPath, whose pretraining spans more than one
billion patches under a slide-level aggregator [ 4 ] . H-optimus-0
supplies an independently pretrained self-supervised view at large
scale [ 5 ] , while CONCH aligns
histology with language via vision-language pretraining [ 3 ] . Although
these models cut downstream training cost and frequently transfer well, they
are far from interchangeable: disparities in pretraining data, architecture,
objective, magnification, and output space produce distinct morphological
priors and distinct failure modes. Representational-similarity analyses
corroborate that the encoders occupy measurably separate feature
spaces [ 19 ] . The best-performing
foundation model accordingly shifts with the dataset and the evaluation target,
which renders it natural to regard several models as complementary views of one
slide.

blocks.en: II-B Multiple Instance Learning for WSI Classification
blocks.zh: II-B WSI分类的多例学习

blocks.en:
WSI classification is routinely posed as multiple-instance
learning, in which a slide forms a bag of patch embeddings and only the slide
label is observed. Attention-based MIL introduced a simple yet effective
trainable aggregation scheme [ 1 ] , and
subsequent methods such as CLAM, DSMIL, and TransMIL strengthened weakly
supervised learning and long-range aggregation [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] . A
parallel thread renders MIL uncertainty-aware, for example through evidential
instance modeling or probabilistic bag embeddings [ 12 , 17 ] , yet
each such method still operates inside a single feature space. A more recent
view holds that the principal bottleneck in the foundation-model era lies in
the training and aggregation protocol rather than the encoder; nnMIL answers
this by offering a generalizable MIL scaffold equipped with randomized patch
and feature sampling, sliding-window inference, and built-in uncertainty
estimation [ 2 ] . Throughout this study nnMIL
serves as a consistent training and inference backbone across all feature
spaces. Fixing the MIL pipeline guarantees that the dominant source of
variation is the foundation-model representation together with the confidence
fusion strategy rather than the aggregator.

blocks.en: II-C Foundation Model Fusion and Open Uncertainty Problem
blocks.zh: II-C 基础模型合并和开放不确定性问题

blocks.en:
Since prediction quality is not monopolized by any one
encoder, recent work fuses heterogeneous pathology representations to lift
slide classification. Classical ensembling, which combines independently
trained predictors, is a well-established route to improved
calibration [ 25 ] , and
pathology-specific fusion has carried the idea further. FuseCPath merges
multi-scale heterogeneous FMs via cluster-level patch re-embedding and
slide-level distillation to yield a stronger ensemble [ 20 ] , and
multimodal slide foundation models integrate several representation streams in
pursuit of accuracy [ 21 ] . These efforts confirm that heterogeneity is a usable resource, yet their orientation remains primarily accuracy-driven, typically homogenizing multi-view variance into a singular representation. Separately,
uncertainty estimation for WSI classification has been examined mostly within
one representation, through MC dropout, conformal prediction, or probabilistic
MIL [ 13 , 10 , 14 , 15 , 11 , 16 , 12 , 17 ] . The
two bodies of literature consequently stay largely disjoint. Once several
competitive foundation models are on hand, the open issue is not merely how to
fuse them for better prediction but also how to quantify uncertainty where
their evidence conflicts, given that naive probability pooling inherently smooths out the epistemic dissonance most diagnostic of borderline cases. Uncertainty within foundation-model
fusion thus remains open and insufficiently addressed, and it is precisely this
problem that the present paper targets

blocks.en: III Method
blocks.zh: 页:1 方法

blocks.en: III-A Problem Setup
blocks.zh: 三-A 问题设置

blocks.en:
Let x x be a WSI with slide label y ∈ { 1 , … , C } y\in\{1,\dots,C\} , and let F F pathology foundation models each define their own feature space and nnMIL
classifier [ 2 ] . Each FM has its own nnMIL classifier, trained separately for the downstream task. CaliFuse is applied only afterward: it does not update the FM encoders or retrain those classifiers. “Training-free” refers only to this fusion and confidence stage. blocks.en: IV-A Datasets and Preprocessing
blocks.zh: 数据集和预处理

blocks.en:
We evaluate CaliFuse on seven WSI classification tasks spanning two
clinically distinct problem types: tumor subtyping, which distinguishes
histological or molecular subtypes within a cancer type, and
biomarker-derived classification, where class labels are defined by
molecular or receptor-status endpoints with direct therapeutic relevance.
Counts, class numbers, and the evaluation split are in Table I .
The five cross-validated tasks are drawn from TCGA (KIDNEY, SARC, BLCA, BRCA, and LGG/GBM). EBRAINS-11 and EBRAINS-30 come from the EBRAINS Digital Brain Tumour Atlas.

EBRAINS-11 and EBRAINS-30 share one cohort: the former collapses 30 WHO classes
into 11 broad categories, and the latter keeps the full taxonomy.

blocks.en: IV-B Foundation Models and Experimental Protocol

blocks.en:
We do not assume that the five feature spaces are aligned or share the
same dimensionality; nnMIL reads each exported HDF5 feature bag in its
native dimension. CaliFuse then consumes the resulting slide-level probability vectors together with chunk-level class distributions. For each extractor and each task, nnMIL trains a
SimpleMIL model under five-fold cross-validation, so both training and nnMIL inference scale with N N ; each extractor keeps its own checkpoint. CaliFuse adds no further trained module. The HDF5 bags it reads are offline features, counted as preprocessing rather than as fusion time. During fold k k , only slides assigned
to fold k k are used as the test set, and all metrics are computed for
that fold before averaging across folds. The training wrapper uses batch
size 32, learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and up to
100 epochs unless otherwise noted.

blocks.en: IV-C Metric Design and Interpretation
blocks.zh: IV-C 计量设计和口译

blocks.en:
Our central claim is that CaliFuse , by fusing multiple
foundation-model views, improves confidence estimation relative to any
single feature, while balanced accuracy stays competitive rather than being traded away. We report six metrics, fixed throughout the paper: ECE,
Brier score, AUROC, AUPR, AURC, and balanced accuracy (Bacc). ECE measures
calibration as the bin-wise gap between predicted confidence and
empirical accuracy. Brier score evaluates the squared error of the full
predictive distribution per sample, penalizing confident wrong
predictions. AUROC measures whether confidence ranks correct predictions
above incorrect ones; AUPR evaluates the same ranking property under
class imbalance. AURC sorts slides by confidence and accumulates risk as
more slides are accepted, so a low AURC means errors concentrate among
low-confidence slides. Bacc depends only on predicted labels, guarding
against apparent gains in these metrics that come from degrading the
classifier itself.
For every metric, we compare CaliFuse against the best single extractor for that
metric (oracle, O) and against a naive ensemble (E), which averages both
the slide-level probability vectors and the per-slide confidence scores
of all five extractors and takes the arg-max class.

blocks.en: IV-D Main Results
blocks.zh: 四-D 主要成果

blocks.en:
Table II reports the N = 5 N{=}5 setting (best value per row in bold).
On EBRAINS-30, the largest multi-class task, AURC is the most informative metric since the system must rank high-risk slides lower in the review queue amid heavy class competition. Our CaliFuse reduces AURC by 33.7% and 36.8% relative to the single-extractor oracle and naive ensemble, respectively, and also improves ECE (63.6%), Brier (3.7%), AUROC (19.5%), and AUPR (7.4%) over the oracle, confirming that cross-view disagreement is especially valuable when class competition is high. GBM/LGG further shows the gains hold under merged cohorts: relative to the oracle, ECE, Brier, AUROC, AUPR, and AURC improve by 53.5%, 7.5%, 16.4%, 5.4%, and 36.6%, respectively. BRCA-TNBC offers a complementary binary, biomarker-driven setting, where AUPR and AUROC best reflect positive-class recognition and discrimination. Our CaliFuse improves AUPR and AUROC by 4.2% and 14.5% over the oracle and by 7.2% and 36.7% over the naive ensemble, confirming the CaliFuse estimate generalizes to binary biomarker classification.

blocks.en: IV-E What the Results Mean for the Pipeline
blocks.zh: 四-E 输油管结果如何

blocks.en:
The results separate two conclusions. First, on balanced accuracy, simply
using multiple features (naive ensemble) already outperforms the
single-extractor oracle, showing that more views help accuracy. Second,
this advantage does not carry over to uncertainty: on the five
calibration and error-ranking metrics (ECE, Brier, AUROC, AUPR, AURC), the
naive ensemble
shows no consistent gain over the oracle, and sometimes performs worse.
Our CaliFuse closes this gap, clearly outperforming both the
single-extractor oracle and the naive ensemble on all five calibration and
error-ranking metrics.

blocks.en: V Discussion and Limitations
blocks.zh: 五. 讨论和限制

blocks.en:
The findings imply that heterogeneous foundation models are
valuable beyond the classification features they contribute: they also expose
multi-view disagreement from which confidence can be built. A lone extractor
may be accurate yet brittle, assigning a high softmax score even where
differing foundation-model views or chunk-level evidence fail to endorse the
same decision. The CaliFuse fusion score is engineered to systematically penalize multi-view epistemic mismatch, which explains why the
sharpest gains land in AUROC and AURC, the metrics that directly test whether
confidence can push likely errors lower in the review queue.

blocks.en: Limitations: the gains require the N N trained FM–nnMIL branches, so cost grows with N N ; each N N is evaluated on a single FM subset; EBRAINS-11 and EBRAINS-30 come from one official split and are reported without fold variance; and λ = 0.5 \lambda{=}0.5 is fixed rather than tuned per task. A natural extension appends a validation-set calibration layer after fusion, such as temperature scaling [ 8 ] , when a deployment needs the scores to read as calibrated probabilities of correctness.

blocks.en: VI Conclusion
blocks.zh: 六. 结论

blocks.en:
This paper has established that heterogeneity across pathology
foundation models, long dismissed as a nuisance to be fused away, can instead be
measured and turned into calibrated confidence. CaliFuse accomplishes this
through two training-free measures operating at separate levels, Multi-FM
Decision Consensus Confidence and Multi-FM Chunk-Level Evidence Confidence,
which jointly capture slide-level decision agreement and chunk-level evidence
consistency. Experiments over seven WSI tasks confirm that representational
disagreement serves as a useful signal for calibrated confidence estimation,
advancing calibration, error ranking, and selective prediction beyond single-FM
and naive ensemble baselines while retaining competitive classification
accuracy.
